d.g: Having been or happened in the distant past.
An event that happened in the past.
An object from the past; a relic, antique, etc.

bygone.e: English by English gone English bygone From by (adverb) + gone.

d.g: past
d.x: The Hospital […] for these two bypast years has contained not less than 150 beds, generally occupied by a full amount of patients.

d.g: Alternative letter-case form of Byzantine (figurative senses only).
A byzant (coin).
Near or next to.
d.x: The mailbox is by the bus stop.

d.g: From one side of something to the other, passing close by; past.
d.x: The stream runs by our back door.

d.g: Not later than (the given time); not later than the end of (the given time interval); before.
After a given amount of time has elapsed or a given event has occurred.
d.x: By February, we were all sick of the cold.

by.e: From Middle English by, bi, from Old English bī (“by; near; around”), from Proto-West Germanic *bī, from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near; by; around; about”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi. …

d.g: an ancient Mediterranean seaport that was a thriving city state in Phoenicia during the second millennium BC;  was the chief port for the export of papyrus;  located in Lebanon to the north of Beirut;  now partially excavated
Any fish (or other creatures) that are not targeted as a catch but are unintentionally caught, and often discarded back into the sea.
d.x: Some offer him bags of bycatch—fish too small or net-mangled to sell, rays and seahorses few will want, and so on.

d.g: Any person, animal, or thing, captured unintentionally on camera or film.
To catch unintentionally while fishing for something else.

bycatch.e: English by- Vulgar Latin captus Proto-Indo-European *-yetider. Vulgar Latin -io Vulgar Latin *captiāre Old French chacierbor. Anglo-Norman cachierbor. Middle English cacchen English catch English bycatch From by- + catch.

d.g: an industrial city and river port in northern Poland

The position of a person or team in a tournament or competition who draws no opponent in a particular round so advances to the next round unopposed, or is awarded points for a win in a league table; also the phantom opponent of such a person or team.
d.x: Craig's Crew plays the bye next week.

d.g: An extra scored when the batsmen take runs after the ball has passed the striker without hitting either the bat or the batsman.
An unspecified way or place.
d.x: Frank Kennedy will shew you the penalties in the act, and ye ken yoursell they used to put their run goods into the auld Place of Ellangowan up bye there.

d.g: A pass.

bye.e: Variant form of by, from Old English bī (“being near”).

d.g: a landlocked republic in eastern Europe;  formerly a European soviet
a landlocked republic in eastern Europe;  formerly a European soviet
a native or inhabitant of Byelorussia
A local custom or law of a settlement or district.
A rule made by a local authority to regulate its own affairs.
A numbered provision within such kind of legislation.
A law or rule governing the internal affairs of an organization (e.g., corporation or business).

bylaw.e: From Middle English bylawe, bilawe, partly from Old English bīlage (“bylaw”) and partly from a variant of Middle English byrelawe, birlawe, from Old Norse býjar (“town's; settlement's”) + lǫg (“laws; jurisdiction”). …

d.g: Synonym of epithet, a descriptive and distinguishing additional name.
d.x: Lions-heart, is... the by-name of K. Richard.

d.g: A formal epithet for a god or goddess, used in rituals in Heathenry.
Synonym of pseudonym, a second name used to disguise authorship etc.

byname.e: From by- + name. Cognate with Dutch bijnaam (“nickname”), German Beiname (“nickname, epithet”), Swedish binamn, Danish binavn and Norwegian Bokmål binavn.

d.g: A road that passes around something, such as a residential area or business district.
A replacement road for obsolete road that is no longer in use because devastating natural disasters (earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides).
The act of going past or around.
A section of pipe that conducts a fluid around some other fixture.

bypass.e: From Middle English *bypassen, *bipassen (suggested by past participle by-past, bipast), equivalent to by- + pass.

d.g: An unfrequented path; an indirect route; a byway.

bypath.e: Inherited from Middle English bypath; by surface analysis, by + path.

d.g: Any action, carried out onstage during a performance, apart from the main action.
d.x: [...] there had been some amusing byplay with the enginemen as to what might be expected to happen if the engines failed to behave themselves properly.

d.g: Any action, by supporting actor.

byplay.e: English by- English play English byplay From by- + play.

d.g: Alternative form of by-product.

byproduct.e: English by- Proto-Indo-European *per-der.? Proto-Indo-European *per-der.? Proto-Indo-European *pér Proto-Indo-European *-o Proto-Indo-European *pró Proto-Indo-European *pro- Proto-Italic *pro- Latin prō- Proto-Indo-European *dewk- Proto-Indo-European *déwkti Proto-Italic *doukō Latin dūcō Latin prōdūcō Latin prōductusd …

d.g: English organist and composer of church music;  master of 16th century polyphony;  was granted a monopoly in music printing with Thomas Tallis (1543-1623)
A barn, especially one used for keeping cattle in.
d.x:
It was here in the kitchen, in the passage,
In the mews in the harn in the byre in the market-place [...]

byre.e: From Middle English bire, bier, byr, from Old English bȳre.

d.g: A short chain mail shirt, covering from the upper arms to the upper thighs.
d.x: It was the Viking habit. Even as a man plowed his field or chopped trees in the woods, his byrnie and his sword were always at hand.

byrnie.e: From Middle English brinie, burne (whence also, without metathesis, obsolete English brinie), from Old Norse brynja. Cognates include Old English byrne, Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌿𐌽𐌾𐍉 (brunjō) (whence Old Church Slavonic брънѩ (brŭnję)), German Brünne, French broigne.

d.g: A road less frequented than a highway; a byway.

byroad.e: English by- English road English byroad From by- + road.

d.g: English romantic poet notorious for his rebellious and unconventional lifestyle (1788-1824)
The long fine silky filaments excreted by several mollusks (particularly Pinna nobilis) by which they attach themselves to the sea bed, and from which sea silk is manufactured.
Sea silk manufactured from these filaments.
The stipe or stem of some fungi which are particularly thin and thread-like.

byssus.e: From New Latin byssus (“sea silk”), from Latin byssus (“fine cotton or cotton stuff, silk”), from Ancient Greek βύσσος (bússos, “a very fine yellowish flax and the linen woven from it”), from Hebrew בּוּץ (búts), Aramaic בּוּצָא (būṣā).

d.g: A person who, although present at some event, does not take part in it; an observer, witness, or spectator.
A short sequence of bits (binary digits) that can be operated on as a unit by a computer; the smallest usable machine word.
A unit of computing storage equal to eight bits, which can represent any of 256 distinct values.
d.x: The word “hello” fits into five bytes of ASCII code.

byte.e: An alteration of the word bite so it would not be accidentally misspelled as bit. Coined by Werner Buchholz in 1956, during the early design phase for the IBM 7030 Stretch computer.

d.g: A road or track not following a main route; a secondary or minor road or path.
d.x: Near-synonyms: back road, back street, back lane

d.g: A road that is not frequently travelled.
a little-known or arcane field of study or detail.

byway.e: From Middle English bywey, equivalent to by- + way.

d.g: A proverb or proverbial expression, common saying; a frequently used word or phrase.
A characteristic word or expression; a word or phrase associated with a person or group.
Someone or something that stands as an example (i.e. metonymically) for something else, by having some of that something's characteristic traits.
An object of notoriety or contempt, scorn or derision.
d.x: He hath made me also a byword of the people […]

byword.e: From Middle English byword, byworde (“proverb”), from Old English bīword, bīwyrd, bīwyrde (“proverb, household word", also "adverb”), from Proto-West Germanic *bīwurdī, equivalent to by- + word. Compare Latin proverbium, which byword may possibly be a translation of. Cognate with Old High German pīwurti (“proverb”). …

d.g: Alternative form of bezant.
d.x: “Gramercy! good fellow,” cried Prince John, “thou pleasest me—Here, Isaac, lend me a handful of byzants.”

d.g: the doctrine that the state is supreme over the church in ecclesiastical matters
an ancient city on the Bosporus founded by the Greeks;  site of modern Istanbul;  in 330 Constantine I rebuilt the city and called it Constantinople and made it his capital
